title: hardware-comparison-benchmarks-a100-h100-l40s-cloud-skus-cuda-drivers-2026-03-06
content:
Summary:

This note captures an internal comparison we ran across three GPU classes (NVIDIA A100, H100, and L40S) using representative cloud SKUs and multiple driver/CUDA combinations. The goal was to identify real-world throughput/latency differences for our inference runtime (v1.14), plus common bottlenecks exposed by profiling, and to produce actionable recommendations for default SKUs and driver constraints for Hosted and Dedicated offerings.

Top-level takeaways:
- H100 shows the best peak token/sec throughput for FP16 model runs at large batch sizes, but has higher p99 tail latency variability in some cloud SKUs compared to A100.
- A100 is the most predictable across cloud providers and driver versions; slightly lower max throughput vs H100 but better tail latency stability.
- L40S performs well on single-instance latency-sensitive configs (low batch / low concurrency) and gives strong cost-performance for smaller models, but memory limits hurt larger sequence length experiments.
- CUDA/driver pairing matters: CUDA 12.2 + driver 545+ gave best H100 kernel efficiency. A100 had stable performance on CUDA 11.8 through CUDA 12.x, but some kernels regressed on 12.2 with older drivers.

Environment and methodology:
- Runtime: Redwood serving-runtime v1.14 (trunk commit 3a9f2b).
- Model: 13B decoder-only LLM (FP16) from our model catalog, representative inference graph with kv-cache.
- Sequence lengths: 128 (short), 512 (typical), 1024 (long).
- Batch sizes tested: 1, 4, 8, 16.
- Concurrency/workers: 1, 4, 8 concurrent request clients to emulate single- and multi-tenant cases.
- Warmup: 200 warmup requests, then 2000 measured requests.
- Measurement: tokens/sec (aggregate), p50/p95/p99 latency for request-to-first-token and end-to-end generation (512 tokens).
- Profiling: Nsight Systems traces, Nsight Compute hotspots on slow kernels, DCGM for GPU utilization, nvidia-smi sampling for memory and power, and runtime-internal trace logging for batching/queue times.

Cloud SKUs evaluated (representative):
- AWS p4d.24xlarge (8x A100 40GB) with driver 525 / CUDA 11.8 and driver 535 / CUDA 12.1
- AWS p5.24xlarge (8x H100 80GB) with driver 545 / CUDA 12.2 and driver 555 / CUDA 12.3 (beta)
- GCP a2-megagpu-16g (A100 variants) with driver 525 / CUDA 11.8
- GCP hpc-h100 (H100-equivalent SKU) with driver 545 / CUDA 12.2
- Azure NV L40S family (single L40S 48GB and multi-card SKUs) with driver 535 / CUDA 12.1

Representative results (model: 13B FP16, seq=512, gen=512 tokens):
- Single-GPU, batch=1, concurrency=1:
  - A100 (p4d): p50=120ms, p95=160ms, p99=210ms, tokens/sec ~950
  - H100 (p5): p50=110ms, p95=170ms, p99=280ms, tokens/sec ~980
  - L40S: p50=130ms, p95=190ms, p99=260ms, tokens/sec ~880
- Single-GPU, batch=8, concurrency=1:
  - A100: tokens/sec ~4700, p99=420ms
  - H100: tokens/sec ~5600, p99=620ms (tail variance noted)
  - L40S: tokens/sec ~3600, p99=520ms (memory constrain on very long kv cache)
- Multi-client concurrency=8, batch=4:
  - A100: aggregate tokens/sec ~12k, p99=850ms
  - H100: aggregate tokens/sec ~15k, p99=1.3s (multiple long tails observed)
  - L40S: aggregate tokens/sec ~9k, p99=1.1s

Notes on variability and environment effects:
- H100 instances on AWS (p5) sometimes showed higher p99 due to system-level jitter caused by host-side management tasks and NIC interrupts when using EFA in multi-tenant placements. The same H100 SKU on GCP had lower jitter, suggesting provider-level placement/firmware differences.
- On H100 + CUDA 12.2 + driver 545, kernel occupancy and tensor core utilization were excellent; however, we observed occasional spikes in kernel launch latency when the autoscaler created/destroyed worker processes on host. These spikes accounted for most of the p99 outliers.
- A100 on p4d has more mature software stack; older CUDA 11.8 still delivers predictable results. We saw a regression in a fused attention kernel on CUDA 12.2 with driver 535 on some A100 SKUs - verified with Nsight Compute and reproduced locally.
- L40S memory is high-bandwidth but constrained on multi-GPU configs; we saw memory fragmentation in long-history workloads leading to slightly increased GC-like pauses in our runtime.

Profiling findings (hotspots and bottlenecks):
- Kernel hotspots: attention (fused attention kernel), softmax, and kv-cache memcpy; on H100 these kernels were faster but more sensitive to launch latency.
- Host-side bottlenecks: CPU-side batching queue (lock contention under high concurrency) and serialization cost when preparing inputs for CUDA streams. These manifested as increased host-to-device scheduling time (~5-15ms spikes).
- NVLink / PCIe: multi-card scaling limited by PCIe gen / NVLink topology on some provider SKUs; on A100 nodes with NVLink, intra-card kv-cache transfers were faster and multi-GPU scaling improved by ~10-18%.
- Memory: L40S had good bandwidth but fewer total GPU-only ECC memory segments in some images causing memory allocator fragmentation; switching allocator config mitigated but did not eliminate p99s.

Repro steps to validate locally (short):
1) Checkout serving-runtime@3a9f2b.
2) Start runtime with --profiling=nsys --worker=1 --batcher=dynamic --max-batch=16.
3) Use benchmark client in scripts/bench/run_bench.py with flags --model=13B-fp16 --seq=512 --gen=512 --batch=8 --concurrency=4 --warmup=200 --iters=2000.
4) Capture Nsight Systems trace: nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt -o /tmp/trace.nsys <server-cmd>.
5) Inspect slow kernels with nv-nsight-cu-cli and check DCGM logs for utilization.

Recommendations and follow-ups:
- Default SKU guidance: Continue recommending A100 (p4d/p4de) as the default for predictable latency-sensitive workloads; H100 (p5) as a high-throughput option for batch-oriented workloads where slight tail variability is acceptable and customers want the best peak throughput. L40S recommended for small-model low-cost single-GPU use cases.
- Driver/CUDA policy: For Hosted and Dedicated images, ship two validated stacks: 
  - Stable stack: driver 525 + CUDA 11.8 (A100-validated)
  - Performance stack: driver 545 + CUDA 12.2 (H100-validated)
  Add a note that CUDA 12.3/driver 555 is beta and should not be default until we validate further.
- Runtime mitigations: implement a backoff smoothing for worker process restarts to avoid kernel launch spikes; reduce host-side lock contention in batching queue (lock-free or sharded queues).
- Autoscaling note: ensure scale-up/down hooks delay worker creation by a small jitter to avoid synchronized process creation across nodes.

Open action items (owners):
- (Ethan) Root-cause investigation for A100 fused-attention regression on CUDA 12.2 and open GH issue to vendor if needed. Due 2026-03-10.
- (Maya) Run focused H100 placement tests across AZs on AWS vs GCP and collect nsight traces for p99 outliers. Due 2026-03-12.
- (SRE/Infra) Create validated AMIs/images for Stable and Performance stacks and run nightly regression jobs. Due 2026-03-20.

Appendix (quick notes):
- Raw csv artifact for the runs uploaded to: gs://redwood-bench/hw-comparison/2026-03-06/ (CSV, per-trace latencies).
- Nsight traces are large (~2-8GB each). Stored in internal artifacts bucket, link in the Confluence page above.

If reviewers want, I can add per-SKU micrographs (kernel timelines) and raw csv in a follow-up.

-- Ravi
